title: The 3 Most Common Modeling Mistakes Teachers Make achers-make/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies three common mistakes teachers make when modeling routines and directions: providing insufficient detail, projecting a negative or ominous tone, and accepting performance that falls short of what was modeled. He argues good modelers assume nothing, playing out every step from a student's perspective and even adding playful, inconsequential steps to strengthen memory. He warns that a grim or militaristic modeling tone discourages rather than encourages compliance, and that accepting 'good enough' after teaching a standard is the most damaging mistake, since it erodes standards across the board. The piece frames modeling as inseparable from teaching itself, urging teachers to see it as valuable rather than tedious.
points: Teachers often blame students for poor routine-following when the real cause is insufficient detail or clarity in how the routine was modeled.
Good modeling means assuming nothing, playing out every step, and even viewing instruction from the students' physical perspective (e.g., from their desks).
A negative, militaristic tone while modeling discourages rather than encourages attentive, motivated performance.
Accepting performance below what was originally modeled is identified as the most detrimental mistake, since standards erode once 'good enough' is tolerated.
Once a routine has been proven to be performed as modeled, the teacher must hold that standard until the last day of school.
quotes: Yet, it’s an area many teachers struggle with. The truth is, your ability to model what you want and expect from your students in large part determines your success.
They capitalize on the universal desire for students to see with their own eyes what is expected of them—so there are no mysteries or uncertainties, and nothing left uncovered.
Add more details to the mix and your expectations can appear militaristic or mindlessly robotic, which discourages rather than encourages attentiveness, motivation, and good performance.
Regardless of what it is, if you model something for your students, it’s critical you make sure it’s performed as modeled.
Learn to love modeling; to love the beauty of a job well done, the simple, quiet satisfaction of good teaching
